# Problem 1
```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

data("ny_noaa")
head(ny_noaa)
nrow(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)

# Explore dataset
ny_noaa |>
summarize(
missing_prcp = sum(is.na(prcp)),
missing_snow = sum(is.na(snow)),
missing_snwd = sum(is.na(snwd)),
missing_tmax = sum(is.na(tmax)),
missing_tmin = sum(is.na(tmin))
)

# Clean Data
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |>
separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
mutate(
year = as.numeric(year),
month = as.numeric(month),
day = as.numeric(day),
tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
prcp = prcp / 10
)

head(ny_noaa_clean)

```
The NY NOAA dataset has 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. These variables include ID, date, precipitation, snow, snow depth, and maximum and minimum temperature. Multiple variables have missing values, making it a strong issue. The number of missing values for each variable are 145,838 for precipitation, 381,221 for snowfall, 591,786 for snow depth, 1,134,358 for maximum temperature, and 1,134,420 for minimum temperature.

Separate() was used to split the date variable into year, month, and day, and as.numeric() was used to convert them to numeric variables. Maximum and minimum temperature were recorded in tenths of a degree Celsius, so mutate() was used to convert them to numeric and divide them by 10 so they would be in degrees Celsius. Precipitation was also divided by 10 since it was recorded in tenths of a millimeter. Snowfall and snow depth were already in millimeters, so they did not need to be changed.

```{r}
# Most commonly observed snowfall values
ny_noaa_clean |>
group_by(snow) |>
summarize(count = n()) |>
arrange(desc(count))
```

The most commonly observed value for snowfall was 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. This is probably because most days do not have snowfall since it only happens a few days a year in NY. There were also 381,221 missing values. Other values that were commonly observed include 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm. Since they are around 1, 0.5, 2, and 3 inches, snowfall was maybe measured in inches and then converted to millimeters.

```{r, message = FALSE}
# Average max temp in January and July
ny_noaa_temp = ny_noaa_clean |>
filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
mutate(month = case_match(month, 1 ~ "January", 7 ~ "July")) |>
group_by(id, year, month) |>
summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE))

# Two-panel plot with average max temp
ny_noaa_temp |>
drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
facet_grid(. ~ month) +
labs(
x = "Year",
y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)",
title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July")
```

The average maximum temperature is lower in January when compared to July. In January, temperatures are typically around -5°C to 5°C. However, in July, temperatures are around 25°C to 30°C. There is no clear trend in temperatures across years, they seem stable. In addition, there are a few outliers with lower than normal temperatures in both January and July.


```{r, warning = FALSE, fig.asp = 1.4}
# tmax vs tmin for the full dataset
ggp_tmax_tmin = ny_noaa_clean |>
ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
geom_hex() +
labs(
title = "Max vs min temperature",
x = "Min temperature (C)",
y = "Max temperature (C)"
)

# Snowfall distribution between 0 - 100 mm
ggp_snow = ny_noaa_clean |>
filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
geom_boxplot() +
labs(
title = "Snowfall distribution (0 - 100 mm)",
x = "Snowfall (mm)",
y = "Year"
)

# Combine plots
ggp_tmax_tmin / ggp_snow
```

Geom_hex() was used since there were too many observations for a scatterplot to be readable. Maximum and minimum temperature had a positive relationship, so days with higher minimum temperatures also had higher maximum temperatures. Most observations were between about -10°C and 15°C for minimum temperature and 0°C and 30°C for maximum temperature. There were a few outliers, like temperatures around 60°C and -60°C, which could have been data errors. Geom_boxplot() was used to show snowfall between 0 and 100 mm for each year. The distribution was similar across the years, with a median of around 25 mm.

# Problem 2 
```{r}
# Demographic data
nhanes_covar = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("NA", ".", "")) |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
filter(age >= 21) |>
drop_na() |>
mutate(
sex = case_match(sex, 1 ~ "male", 2 ~ "female"),
sex = factor(sex),
education = case_match(education,
1 ~ "Less than high school",
2 ~ "High school equivalent",
3 ~ "More than high school"),
education = factor(education, levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"))
)

# Accelerometer data
nhanes_accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
pivot_longer(min1:min1440, names_to = "minute", names_prefix = "min", values_to = "mims") |>
mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

# Merge
nhanes_df = left_join(nhanes_covar, nhanes_accel, by = "seqn")

head(nhanes_df)
```
The first 4 rows of the demographic data were skipped since they had descriptions of the variables. Participants under 21 and those with missing demographic data were removed using filter() and drop_na(). Case_match() and factor() were used to make sex and education categorical, and education was ordered as less than high school, high school equivalent, and more than high school so it would show in that order in tables and plots instead of alphabetical order. Pivot_longer() was used to change the 1,440 minute columns into rows, so each participant had one row for each minute of the day with the activity value for that minute. Left_join() was used to merge the datasets by participant ID. The final dataset had `r nrow(nhanes_covar)` participants and `r nrow(nhanes_df)` rows.

```{r}
# Number of men and women in each education category
nhanes_covar |>
count(education, sex) |>
pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
knitr::kable()

# Age distribution for men and women in each education category
nhanes_covar |>
ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
geom_boxplot() +
facet_grid(. ~ education) +
labs(
title 

= "Age distribution by sex and education",
x = "Sex",
y = "Age (years)"
)
```
Count(), pivot_wider(), and knitr::kable() were used to make a table of the number of men and women in each education category. Most participants were in the "More than high school" category, with 59 women and 56 men. The "Less than high school" category had a similar number of women and men (28 and 27), but the "High school equivalent" category had more men than women (35 and 23). Geom_boxplot() and facet_grid() were used to show the age distribution for men and women in each education category. Participants in the "More than high school" category were younger than the other two categories, with median ages of around 40 years. In the "Less than high school" category, men and women had similar ages, with median ages of around 60 years. In the "High school equivalent" category, women were older than men, with a median age of approximately 62 compared to approximately 53 years.
